1.blurb: The Phoenicians developed their consonant-only writing system around 1050 BCE and spread it across the Mediterranean through their trading network. The Greeks borrowed the letter forms and added vowels, creating the first true alphabet — a transformation that made Greek literature, philosophy, and science possible.

The Mycenaean palace civilization collapsed around 1200 BCE as part of the broader Bronze Age Collapse. The palace bureaucracies, the Linear B writing system, and the centralized economies all vanished within a generation, plunging Greece into a three-century Dark Age.

The Shang dynasty developed Chinese writing through oracle bone divination around 1200 BCE, roughly contemporary with the Mycenaean Linear B tablets. Both writing systems served palace bureaucracies, but Chinese writing survived its dynasty's fall while Linear B died with the Mycenaean palaces.
Greek history opens in the rubble of the Mycenaean collapse — the Dark Age after the citadels fell, from which the polis world would slowly emerge.
The Greeks were latecomers: cities, writing, and kingship were already ancient in Mesopotamia when Greece was still villages of subsistence farmers.
The single most consequential Greek borrowing was the alphabet — adapted from the Phoenician script, vowels added, and turned into the writing system of European literacy.
At the other end of Eurasia, Bronze Age China under the Shang had its own script and ritual-bronze elite — civilization arising independently while Greece was in its dark age.

The Megarian colony of Byzantion would become Constantinople in 330 CE — Constantine's eastern capital and the imperial city that carried the Roman empire forward for another thousand years after the Latin west collapsed.

The horse-riding nomads of the Pontic steppe controlled the grasslands north of the Black Sea. Greek colonists on the Crimean coast became their permanent trading partners — grain and gold flowed south, Greek wine and pottery north — making the steppe and the polis world economic siblings.

When Croesus consulted Delphi, the empire he was thinking of attacking was Cyrus the Great's freshly assembled Achaemenid superstate — the largest the world had yet seen. The oracle's famous ambiguity ('you will destroy a great empire') hid the answer: the great empire was his own. Cyrus rolled over Lydia in 547 BCE.

By the 7th century BCE, Saite-dynasty Egypt was actively recruiting Greek mercenaries and granting Greek traders a permanent settlement at Naucratis on the Nile delta. The contact ran both ways: Greek colonists brought Egyptian mathematics, monumental stone sculpture, and (later) the Egyptian gods' iconography back into the Aegean.

2.blurb: Darius I built the most sophisticated imperial administration the world had seen: twenty satrapies, the Royal Road courier system, standardized coinage, and codified law. Athens' democratic experiment and Persia's bureaucratic monarchy represented two radically different answers to the same question — how do you govern a diverse population?

The Zhou Dynasty's Warring States period was producing its own political fragmentation and intellectual ferment at the same time Athens was inventing democracy. Confucius, like Solon, sought institutional solutions to social crisis — but Confucius looked to restored ritual hierarchy while Solon expanded political participation.
As Athens experimented with citizen government, the Persian Empire was perfecting the opposite model — a vast multi-ethnic bureaucratic monarchy run by satraps and the King's roads.

India's 'sixteen great realms' of the 7th-5th centuries BCE included monarchies and gana-sanghas — oligarchic republics governed by clan-elder councils that debated and voted, the closest non-Greek parallel to Athenian assembly politics in the same era.

By the 6th century BCE Babylonian scribes had been doing sophisticated algebra, square-root approximation, and Pythagorean-theorem geometry on clay tablets for over a thousand years. The Ionians inherited a mathematical inheritance, but reframed it as 'what is reality made of?' rather than 'how do I solve this practical problem?'

Old Babylonian mathematics (c. 1800 BCE) understood the geometric relationship between the legs and hypotenuse of a right triangle more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born — though Babylonians used it as a calculation recipe, not a deductively proved theorem.

3.blurb: Cyrus the Great built the Persian Empire from scratch in fifteen years, conquering Media, Lydia, and Babylon. His conquest of the Lydian kingdom in 547 BCE brought the Greek cities of the Ionian coast under Persian rule, setting up the collision between Greece and Persia that defined the next century.

Darius I responded to the Ionian Revolt by sending the punitive expedition that was defeated at Marathon. From the Persian perspective, Greece was a minor frontier problem — a handful of small cities on the western fringe of an empire stretching from Egypt to the Indus.
The Persian Wars pit the young Greek poleis against the superpower Cyrus and Darius had built — the largest empire the world had yet seen, stopped at Marathon and Salamis.

4.blurb: After Xerxes' failed invasion, Persia turned to managing its still-vast empire — Egypt to the Indus — and to using gold rather than armies to keep the Greek world divided. The Delian League formed against a Persia that remained the great power across the Aegean, even as Athens stopped seeing it as the immediate threat.

Empedocles' four-elements theory (earth, water, air, fire) became the orthodoxy of Western natural philosophy for two thousand years, surviving through Aristotle and the medieval universities until Robert Boyle and the 17th-century chemists finally dismantled it during the Scientific Revolution.

5.blurb: Persia, sensing opportunity after the Sicilian disaster, started funneling gold to Sparta to build a fleet that could beat Athens. Cyrus the Younger — the Persian prince running the western satrapies — was the one cutting the checks. A few years later he would try (and fail) to take the Persian throne for himself, in the campaign Xenophon turned into the Anabasis.

6.blurb: Xenophon's march of the Ten Thousand in 401 BCE proved that a small Greek army could penetrate deep into the Persian Empire and survive. Philip of Macedon and his son Alexander both studied the lesson: Persia's vast territory was not as impregnable as it appeared.

The Persian Empire (the Achaemenid dynasty founded by Cyrus the Great) was still the largest state in the world in the 4th century BCE. Its long afternoon was an empire that had stopped expanding, plagued by satrap revolts and Egyptian secessions but still rich, vast, and capable of raising enormous armies — the prize Philip and Alexander were already eyeing.

By the 4th century BCE Persia had become the arbiter of Greek affairs — funding whichever side served its interest, dictating the King's Peace of 387 BCE, and watching the city-states exhaust themselves. The Achaemenid machinery was running but the bolts were loose: rich and vast, but no longer cohesive.

Persian gold and Persian diplomacy shaped the 4th-century Greek world. Lysander cultivated Persian connections; Xenophon's Ten Thousand marched into a Persian civil war; Philip's invasion plan targeted Persian territory. The Long Afternoon empire was wealthy enough to bankroll every faction.

Justinian, the 6th-century Eastern Roman emperor who tried to reconquer the lost western half of the empire, also closed Plato's Academy in 529 CE — ending its nearly 900-year run as the first institution of higher learning in the Western world.

Alexander the Great, Philip's son and Aristotle's pupil, would carry out his father's planned invasion of Persia and topple the Achaemenid Empire in just over a decade — a campaign whose Persian-side story is told in persian-empire chapter 5.

7.blurb: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 322 BCE, roughly contemporary with Alexander's conquests. While Alexander imposed Greek culture by military force, Chandragupta built an Indian imperial system from the Arthashastra's playbook — ruthless pragmatism applied to subcontinental unification.

Alexander's seven-month siege of Tyre in 332 BCE destroyed the greatest Phoenician city and ended Phoenician independence. The causeway he built to reach the island fortress silted up over the centuries, permanently turning Tyre from an island into a peninsula.

Alexander dismantled the Achaemenid Empire in four years of campaigning, burning Persepolis and declaring himself the legitimate successor of the Persian kings. The empire Cyrus had built in fifteen years and Darius had organized into the ancient world's most efficient bureaucracy was gone.

Alexander reached the Indus region in 326 BCE, fighting King Porus at the Hydaspes. The Indus Valley had been the site of one of humanity's earliest urban civilizations over two thousand years earlier — Alexander was marching through lands with a history as deep as Egypt's.
Alexander's invasion of the Indus directly triggered the Maurya Empire: Chandragupta rose in the vacuum the Macedonians left, building India's first great empire on the Greek frontier.

By Alexander's day, Persia was the Achaemenid super-state Darius I had organized two centuries earlier — satraps governing 20 provinces, royal roads carrying messengers from Sardis to Susa, tribute flowing in from Egypt to the Indus. Alexander didn't have to invent imperial machinery. He inherited it.

The Phoenician city-states had been the Mediterranean's traders and shipbuilders for a thousand years, supplying Persia's fleet under contract. Alexander's siege of Tyre in 332 BCE shattered the largest of them; Phoenicia as an independent civilization ended here.

8.blurb: Ptolemy I seized Egypt after Alexander's death and founded a dynasty that would rule for nearly three centuries. The Ptolemies built Alexandria into the Mediterranean's greatest city, constructed the Library and the Lighthouse, and ruled as pharaohs — Greek kings performing Egyptian rituals in Egyptian temples.

The Seleucid Empire inherited the vast eastern territories of Alexander's conquests but gradually shrank as the Parthians seized Persia and eastern provinces broke away. The Seleucids' failure to hold Alexander's empire proved that military conquest without cultural integration is unsustainable.

Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler, was the final chapter of the Hellenistic age Alexander had inaugurated. Her defeat at Actium in 31 BCE ended Greek rule in Egypt and made the entire Mediterranean a Roman lake — closing the era of independent Greek and Hellenistic kingdoms.

Rome destroyed Carthage in the same year (146 BCE) it destroyed Corinth, ending both Phoenician and Greek political independence in a single devastating season. The coincidence was not lost on ancient observers — the Mediterranean's two oldest trading civilizations were crushed simultaneously by the rising Roman superpower.
Aristarchus had the right answer eighteen centuries before anyone could prove it; the proof, and the fight over it, is the opening of the Scientific Revolution (Scientific Revolution Ch 2).

The Mouseion is the deepest precedent for the scientific society — and the thing the Royal Society pointedly differs from: Alexandria died with its dynasty, the Society was built to outlive any patron (Scientific Revolution Ch 11).
The Hellenistic kingdoms were swallowed one by one by Rome — Greek culture conquered its conqueror, but Greek political independence ended on Roman terms.

Mesopotamia had been the Persian heartland's western half; after Alexander it passed to the Seleucids, then the Parthians — the long handoff from native rule to a sequence of foreign empires that this chapter closes.
Persia, the empire Alexander had broken, became Seleucid territory and then slipped away to the Parthians — the unwinding of Achaemenid Persia and the eastern half of Alexander's legacy.

The Buddha's teachings had spread across India under the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, whose missions reached as far as the Hellenistic courts — the cultural traffic that ran both ways and produced the Greco-Buddhist sculpture of Gandhara.
The Italian Renaissance is, among other things, the rediscovery of the Hellenistic inheritance — geometry, anatomy, philosophy, sculpture — that Greek scholars carried west when Constantinople fell.

Carthage was a Phoenician foundation — the western outpost of a trading civilization that had stretched from Lebanon to the Atlantic. Rome destroyed it in the same year, 146 BCE, that it destroyed Corinth.
The Byzantines — the Greek-speaking Roman Empire that outlasted the West by a thousand years — preserved Greek learning through the medieval centuries when most of Western Europe could not read it.

Byzantine scriptoriums copied and protected most of the classical Greek texts that survive today; when Constantinople fell in 1453, Greek scholars carried those manuscripts to Italy and helped seed the Renaissance.
Medieval Constantinople was the great library of the Greek inheritance — its scriptoriums copied the classical texts the West had lost, and its scholars carried them to Italy after 1453.
The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine state — and triggered the westward flight of Greek scholars whose manuscripts helped ignite the Italian Renaissance.
